The specification is a design proposal: this paper does not yet measure the loss against a live multi-miner metagraph (see Section 8). Miner output. A miner i emits, for each query, a pair mi = (pi , ci ), (1) where pi ∈ [0, 1] is the predicted probability of the realised event over the scoring window ∆, and ci ∈ [0, 1] is the miner’s self-stated calibration confidence in pi .

Material chain-state event. The realised event indicator y ∈ {0, 1} is set to 1 if any of four event classes occurs within ∆ of the prediction emission: E1 , a route-level liquidity contraction beyond a configured threshold; E2 , a price drop beyond a configured threshold over a configured sub-window; E3 , a bridge or oracle anomaly registered by the cross-source redundancy check of Section 3; E4 , a governance state change recorded on-chain. The thresholds and the union over E1 –E4 together define the resolver.

Validator loss. The validator-side loss for miner i is the convex combination

Li = α · Brier(pi , y) + β · Inconsistency(mi ) + γ · Calibration(ci ), α + β + γ = 1. (2)

The Brier component is the squared error Brier(p, y) = (p − y)2 and penalises both wrong predictions and overconfidence. The inconsistency component Inconsistency(mi ) penalises drift across paired queries that share the same chain-state context (no material change between query times). The calibration component Calibration(ci ) is the per-bin gap between stated confidence ci and realised accuracy over the past W paired (ci , y) samples (Section 2).

Defaults. We propose α = 0.6, β = 0.2, γ = 0.2 as the design starting point. The Brier component carries the largest weight because it is the only component grounded directly in realised outcomes; the inconsistency and calibration components are intended to be hard to game without also producing accurate forecasts. Every symbol is declared on first use: mi , pi , ci , y, ∆, α, β, γ, W , E1 –E4 .

5 Case Study: A Policy-Constrained Liquidity Stress-Response Experiment We instrument the scenario engine on a single Solana micro-cap pool between 2026-05-06 01:04 UTC and 2026-05-07 03:44 UTC. The experiment has three phases. Across two stop-loss events the role contract held, and every cap-raise was preceded by a recorded out-of-band approval before the policy boundary widened.

role contract held, and every cap-raise was preceded by a recorded out-of-band approval before the policy boundary widened. Setup. RYA is the RayaChain protocol token. On Solana it trades on a single Raydium constant-product pool (the product of the two reserve quantities is held constant by the pricing function, so larger trades move the price more), launched 2026-05-05 with 37 SOL of seed liquidity. The execution wallet is a hot wallet funded outside the treasury, Squads multisig, and deployer-key custody, and operates under a Trader-role constitution whose hard rules are

buy-only, never use the deployer wallet, live mode requires two flags plus a board sign-off recorded in the issue thread, cap raises require a written rationale and explicit board approval, and no human impersonation. The policy fires a 0.10 SOL buy (five 0.02 SOL slices over 150 s of time-weighted slicing) when price falls below the bottom tier of a four-tier action ladder, with a 600-second cooldown. A daily cap bounds exposure per UTC day; a stop-loss circuit auto-pauses the engine on a 30% drop within a 600-second window.

Phase I — 2026-05-06, first stress event and policy-bound intervention. A stress event was registered at T0 = 01:00 UTC: RYA had drifted approximately −60.9% over the trailing 24 hours, and pool liquidity had moved from a baseline of approximately USD 6,098 to USD 5,418. A manual governance escalation was recorded on the issue thread, the wallet was topped up by 5.000 SOL, and the first policy-bound buy fired at T0 + 4 minutes at price USD 5.679×10−5 . A second escalation at T0 + 7 minutes raised the daily cap from 1.0 to 3.0 SOL with a written rationale. Twenty-nine further buys completed at the bottom of the ladder; the ratchet primitive raised the bottom-tier price by 50 basis points between buys 8 and 9, and again between buys 28 and 29, when cumulative spend crossed 2.0 SOL and 4.0 SOL respectively. By 06:13 UTC the daily cap bound at exactly 3.000 SOL. Price recovered from USD 5.679×10−5 to USD 6.785×10−5 (+19.5%); pool liquidity returned to USD 6,098. A first non-policy-driven buyer printed at the reconverged price level around 10:00 UTC.

Phase II — 2026-05-06/07, second stress event and ratchet step 3. A second stress event was registered at T1 = 21:15 UTC with magnitude −5.84% over approximately one hour, shaving liquidity from USD 6,071 to USD 5,911. A third escalation at T1 + 15 minutes raised the daily cap from 3.0 to 5.0 SOL, and the policy fired its 31st buy at price USD 6.591×10−5 . Twenty-one further buys completed across the UTC date boundary; ratchet step 3 fired at buy fifty-one (2026-05-07 00:42:18 UTC) when lifetime spend crossed 6.0 SOL. The fifty-second buy completed at 01:14:12 UTC at price USD 7.385×10−5 — the same level at which the prior phase’s first non-policy-driven buyer had printed, now bracketed by a higher ladder.

Phase III — 2026-05-07 02:38 UTC, the stop-loss event. A single sell pushed price USD 0.0000769 → 0.0000414 (−46% in approximately 3–10 minutes), draining roughly USD 1,666 of pool liquidity. The stop-loss circuit auto-paused the engine per the configured 30% drop in a 600-second window — exactly as designed. The safety circuit firing here is a feature of the architecture, not an embarrassment. The stop-loss exists precisely to prevent the role contract from continuing to spend on a pool whose state has changed faster than the policy assumed. At 03:44 UTC a manual governance escalation was recorded on the same issue thread that authorised the original live flip, and the engine was resumed under bounded execution at the new USD 0.0000414 price floor. Daily spend at the resumption moment was 1.46/5.0 SOL and lifetime spend was 7.205 SOL; the wallet held 5.793 SOL post-top-up; the stop-loss circuit was re-armed at the new liquidity baseline of approximately USD 4,661. The experiment continues at the time of writing.

Properties demonstrated by the experiment. Three properties of the scenario engine running under a constitutional agentic-engine constraint can be read directly from the run: (i) the safety circuit trips on its threshold, not only at design time; (ii) the human-in-the-loop escalation path is documented on the same surface that authorised the original live flip, so a third-party auditor can reconstruct the entire decision chain from the public issue thread plus the public decision log; (iii) the role contract holds across two stop-loss events and three out-of-band escalations without violating any of its hard rules. The companion operator-side narrative [24] carries the buy-by-buy decision log (52 rows of timestamps, prices, tier-trigger values, and slice-level execution records).

The April 2026 live-API baseline on the broader production cohort (not shown here) is approximately 53.15% (“barely above chance” [14]), against which the 168-hour evaluation cohort is a more concentrated subset.

What the headline numbers mean and do not mean. The 99.34% accuracy on the 2026-05-07 168-hour cohort, taken in isolation, is suspiciously high for a binary risk classifier. Three caveats apply simultaneously: 1. Class imbalance. The outcome resolver is bounded to the top 1,000 assets by market capitalisation [14], a low base-rate cohort. A classifier that says “no crash” most of the time achieves a very high directional accuracy on this cohort almost by definition. 2. The Brier calibration error is the metric that survives. Perfect = 0, marginal-50/50 prior = 0.25; our value = 0.1335 sits closer to perfect than to random but is well short of headline-grade. 3. The 53% live baseline is the right denominator. The comparison that survives is against the broader production cohort, not the narrower 168-hour one. The architectural contribution of this paper is the verification primitive — the calibration arc is the empirical evidence that there is a production telemetry surface against which a verification subnet could meaningfully score miners.

7 Orchestration: Two Layers A verifiable agentic system needs two distinct orchestration layers, and this paper’s contribution depends on keeping them separate. The first is agent-task management: the surface that scopes who is allowed to act and on what terms — role contracts, the paused-by-default stance, and the requirement of an out-of-band human approval recorded on the same audit trail that authorises every action. The second is runtime orchestration: a state machine that walks each agent run through prediction, sentiment fusion, tool invocation, and emission. The deployed instantiation uses LangGraph for the runtime layer and a Paperclip-style task-management service for the contract layer [26]; the architectural claim of this section, however, is the separation itself and not either implementation, because conflating the two layers (one service handling both) collapses the audit trail that makes the agentic engine verifiable. A single hard rule binds the runtime to the contract layer: the runtime cannot bypass the agentic engine’s policy boundary. In our deployment, that surfaces as a prohibition on direct LLM

HTTP paths from runtime nodes; every model invocation routes through an in-process AiRouter so that model selection, fallback, daily-cost limits, and audit logs are respected [26]. Every emission the runtime produces conforms to a strict JSON schema with a validationStatus field in {valid, degraded, fallback}, written append-only to an audit log; downstream consumers refuse any record that fails schema validation. This is a constitutional-AI claim, not a deployment detail: a runtime that can emit unstructured output cannot be verified against a role contract. The runtime ships with a three-tier fallback ladder (remote orchestrator → in-process orchestrator → legacy non-agentic path), so an agent-infrastructure outage degrades the system to a strictly less capable but still-correct mode rather than to a 5xx error [26]. The synthesis layer that composes the five engines into a single agent decision (Strategy Alpha, in the engineering documentation) is the same agentic engine of Section 2, exposed through the runtime’s terminal node; the long-form report carries the deployment-level configuration and test surface that this section deliberately omits.

8 Limitations as Falsification We state the load-bearing limitations as falsification statements: what would have to be observed for the claim to fail, and the smallest experiment that could observe it.

• Single-pool case study. A second run on a different Solana micro-cap pool that fails to reconverge to the pre-stress price under the same role contract would falsify the deployability claim. The smallest experiment is the same scenario engine pointed at any other RYA-tier asset on Solana, with the same buy-only constitution and a ≥2-cycle window. We make no causal claim that the policy caused reconvergence; the natural-experiment counterfactual is unavailable.

• Top-cap cohort restriction on the calibration arc. The 99.34% directional accuracy is on a top-1,000-by-mcap cohort. The smallest experiment that would falsify the broad-cohort claim is to lift the cohort restriction and re-run the 168-hour evaluation; the hypothesis would be falsified if the broad-cohort calibration error climbs above 0.20.

• Validator-loss components are not yet measured at scale. The Bittensor shadow soak validates the orchestration path, but the three components of the validator loss (Brier accuracy + Inconsistency over paired queries with no material chain-state change + Miscalibration via reliability bins) are deferred [13]. The smallest experiment that would break the verification claim is to introduce a second miner with a non-trivial protocol, accumulate (c, y) pairs across realised events, and report the three-component decomposition in a follow-up. Until that runs, the verification claim is architectural, not measured.

A fourth honest disclosure: the agentic engine in the case study is a deterministic Traderrole policy, not the LLM-mediated agentic engine of Section 2. The case study validates the program-registry / trigger-evaluator / constrained-execution decomposition; the LLM-mediated agentic engine is a follow-on build.

accuracy. Resolution-Aware Perpetual Futures on Binary Prediction Markets: An Empirical Risk-Design Framework Using Polymarket Data

Maksym Nechepurenko∗ May 10, 2026

Abstract We ask whether a perpetual-futures engine could have survived observed conditions on

arXiv:2605.10400v1 [q-fin.TR] 11 May 2026 Polymarket’s binary-event prediction markets, and what its design would need to look like if so. We do not propose deployment; the contribution is a specification of a resolution-aware risk-engine framework, an empirical evaluation of that framework as specified, and the design tensions the evaluation reveals. Binary event-contract underlyings have three structural properties absent from cryptoperpetual design assumptions: bounded support with terminal collapse, structurally asymmetric depth near the boundaries, and oracle-mediated discrete resolution. Two non-portability propositions follow: standard basis-only funding paired with continuousvolatility static margin fails to constrain behavior near the boundaries (Proposition 2) and provides insufficient collateral to absorb the bounded-event terminal jump (Proposition 1). The propositions rest on the three structural properties only. We specify a four-component framework: a composite robust index; a jump-aware tiered margin schedule; boundary-aware funding correction; and a multi-stage resolution-zone protocol with leverage compression. Every parameter is either estimated from observable market features with a documented estimator (Section C) or designated a policy parameter and varied in sensitivity analysis (Section E). Estimators and falsifiability thresholds are pre-registered and locked before the empirical evaluation runs. Empirical evaluation uses Polymarket’s PMXT v2 archive for the calendar week 2026- 04-21 to 2026-04-27 (13.7 billion events, 110,828 distinct markets, stratified-by-day analysis sample of 13,298 markets passing adequacy gates, of which 13,115 resolved within the empirical window for E3 evaluation). E1 evaluates two pre-registered stylized facts; E2 conducts counterfactual replay across three engine configurations on observed price paths; E3 isolates the resolution-zone protocol’s contribution by comparing four mechanic variants. Both E1 floors pass; three of the five materiality floors of E2 and E3 fail and two pass. The full numerical results are summarised in Section 1.5 and reported in detail in Section 8. Two design lessons emerge from the failed floors and constitute the empirical contribution. First, the resolution-zone halt protocol addresses execution-channel liquidation risk but does not address terminal-jump bad-debt: bad-debt risk lives in the margin schedule, not the halt protocol. Second, dynamic-margin reaction pre-empts more recoveries than it prevents on observed paths — a structural trade-off replicated across the E2 and E3 counterfactual replays. The framework as specified does not achieve the order-of-magnitude liquidation-rate or bad-debt reduction hypothesized at pre-registration. The empirical evaluation supports directional welfare-side improvement and documents structural design tensions rather than validating the framework. Five framework-conditional design recommendations follow as directions for further empirical work; we do not claim a deployable product.

Keywords: prediction markets; perpetual futures; event contracts; market microstructure; risk design; Polymarket; pre-registration. JEL Classification: G13, G14, G18, G24.

∗ Director of Research, Devnull; [email].

1 Introduction 1.1 Motivation Prediction markets and perpetual futures are converging. Prediction markets, historically a niche academic instrument for aggregating beliefs about future events (Manski, 2006; Wolfers and Zitzewitz, 2004), have grown into public-facing trading venues with material volume; the largest of them, Polymarket, drew widespread public attention around the 2024 US election cycle (see Tsang and Yang, 2026 for transaction-level documentation), and its tick-level public archive is now a research dataset in its own right (Section 3.3). Perpetual futures, in turn, have become the dominant derivative structure in cryptocurrency markets (He et al., 2024): non-expiring, margin-collateralized, with periodic funding payments anchoring the mark price to a reference index. Industry commentary has begun pointing at the convergence directly. In August 2025, John Wang, the head of crypto at Kalshi, summarized the convergence in a much-discussed post:“Perps are Prediction Markets. Prediction Markets are Perps” (Wang, 2025). (industry signal; Section F) The claim, taken literally, is too strong — prediction markets resolve at a known terminal state, perpetual futures do not — but it captures the emerging product question: can perpetual-style margin and funding infrastructure, built for unbounded crypto spot underlyings, be adapted to bounded prediction-market events? The question is not idle. A platform considering a leveraged perpetual product on event markets faces a concrete operational choice: import the engineering of crypto perpetual exchanges directly, or design something new. Importing directly is faster and better understood, but the underlying price process is structurally different (Section 3.1). Designing something new requires a framework that is currently absent from both the academic literature and the public design documents of major platforms.

1.2 The risk-design problem This paper studies that design problem. We refer to a margin-based derivative on a single binary prediction-market event with no fixed expiry as an event-linked perpetual (ELP). The narrow form analyzed here — the Probability-Index Resolution-Aware Perpetual (PIRAP), specified in plan section 4.2 and reproduced in Section 3.2 — is one design among many in the broader taxonomy of event-linked derivatives. We restrict attention to PIRAP in this paper; Section 1.6 states what we exclude and where it is deferred. The central observation is structural: a binary prediction-market price process exhibits four features that distinguish it from unbounded spot underlyings (Section 3.1). Bounded support in [0, 1] replaces unbounded support in R+ . A discrete terminal collapse to {0, 1} at resolution time replaces a continuous trajectory. Jump intensity scales with information arrival, not calendar time. And liquidity in the tails of the unit interval is asymmetrically thin, in a way that depends on the region of the price rather than on its level alone. These features individually appear in other contexts. Bounded processes appear in interestrate modeling. Terminal jumps appear in event-study finance. Information-driven jump intensity appears in high-frequency microstructure. The combination, however, is not addressed by any standard derivative-pricing or risk-engine framework. Section 6 formalizes the gap with two propositions: continuous-volatility margin schedules cannot price terminal jump risk without forcing leverage to one (Proposition 1), and basis-only funding fails to deliver the relative-basis convergence that traders and arbitrageurs rely on, in the boundary regions of the unit interval (Proposition 2). The propositions are structural rather than empirical: they do not demonstrate that the failure modes occur with any particular frequency on observed data. They demonstrate that the naive transplant of crypto-perp mechanics is mathematically incompatible with binary-event

1.3 Approach: empirical survival, not normative product proposal We do not propose a deployable product. We propose the minimum risk architecture under which a deployable product could be empirically evaluated, and we test whether the architecture would have survived observed event-market conditions. Concretely, we use the PMXT v2 public archive of the Polymarket CLOB WebSocket event stream as our empirical backbone (Sections 3.3 and 5). The archive provides tick-level events from 2026-04-13 onward, with millisecond timestamps, order-book snapshots, trade tape, and tick-size changes, in hourly-partitioned Parquet files. The empirical analysis proceeds via counterfactual replay: hypothetical engine configurations are evaluated against observed market paths, with engine outputs computed deterministically from observed inputs and stated rules. Three empirical experiments structure the paper’s evidence base. Experiment E1 (Section 8.1) is descriptive: we document empirical regularities of the binary-event price process on Polymarket. Experiment E2 (Section 8.2) is the central counterfactual: three engine configurations (naive crypto-perp port C0, intermediate C1, full resolution-aware C2) are evaluated under three trader-position assumptions (position-agnostic survivability Section 8.2.1, deterministic position grid Section 8.2.2, calibrated synthetic-trader robustness layer Section 8.2.3). The main empirical claims rest on E2a and E2b, which are trader-independent; E2c is robustness only. Experiment E3 (Section 8.3) compares four resolution-zone protocols on observed pre-resolution windows. The methodology is data-first. Synthetic or Monte Carlo evidence is never primary. The only synthetic element anywhere in the paper is the trader-population layer in E2c, isolated, calibrated to publicly documented crypto-perp leverage histograms, and confined to a robustness role. Section 4 states the ten methodological principles in declarative form before any empirical content appears.

1.4 Contributions The paper makes seven contributions.

1. Empirical microstructure characterization of Polymarket binary-event prices for derivative-design purposes, on the v2 high-frequency event-stream archive. Includes jump-size distribution, spread and depth dynamics conditional on the region of pt within [0, 1], and resolution-time liquidity patterns on a stratified-by-day analysis sample (13,298 usable markets passing adequacy gates from 61,087 ingested across the seven days of the empirical window; 13,115 of these resolved within the empirical window for E3 evaluation, per the sample-progression definitions in Section 5.5). The preregistered Sample Adequacy Gate triggered the sports-dominance consequence rule on the stratified sample (sports share 77.9%, above the 70% threshold), which replicated the trigger that fired on the chronological subsamples and confirmed sports dominance as a structural property of the empirical week’s market mix (Section 5.5). Primary cross-class characterization is therefore sports-anchored; politics and crypto are reported as secondary classes. Cross-class differences are reported with attention to the resolutionwindow structural ceiling of 17.4% (Section 9.7). Section 5.

2. Formal non-portability propositions establishing that standard basis-only funding paired with continuous-vol static margin is structurally insufficient on bounded probability underlyings with terminal collapse. Propositions 1 and 2. Section 6.

3. Resolution-aware risk-engine framework with explicit parameter discipline: every engine input is either estimated from observable market features with a documented estimator, or designated a policy parameter and varied in sensitivity analysis. Estimators and falsifiability thresholds are pre-registered in Section C and locked before empirical experiments are run. Section 7.

4. Three-mode replay-based counterfactual back-test (E2a/E2b/E2c). Main empirical claims are trader-independent. The evaluation is reported transparently regardless of whether pre-registered floors are met; specific calibration findings (e.g., a continuous-vol margin term misspecification documented in Section 9.10) are surfaced as part of the evaluation rather than retroactively absorbed into the framework specification. Section 8.2.

5. Two-tier listing eligibility framework. A Quantitative Suitability Score SEA from observable features, separately from a Governance Overlay BE flagging qualitative integrity concerns. The two are reported separately so that quantitative defensibility is not contaminated by qualitative judgment. Sections 7.8 and 7.9.

6. Reproducibility infrastructure for the PMXT v2 archive. The empirical evaluation in this paper required building a reusable public infrastructure that did not previously exist for systematic Polymarket microstructure research at this scale. Specifically: direct R2 endpoint enumeration of the v2 archive without intermediary services, a sample-selection module with locked seed and stratified-by-day rule (Section 5.5), a run-loop module with mid-stage stop conditions and graceful partial-state preservation (Section D.6), round-robin queue ordering for representative partial samples, persistent HTTP connections in the API enrichment stages, and a SHA manifest discipline that ties every empirical claim back to a specific archive commit. The diagnostic chronological subsamples (Section B.8) document the day-1 selection bias finding that motivated the stratified correction. All code is committed alongside the paper. The infrastructure is reusable: future Polymarket microstructure research can build on it directly rather than re-discover the engineering required to use the v2 archive at scale. Sections B and D.

E1 stylized facts (both pre-registered floors pass). Median boundary depth asymmetry ρpooled = 1.72 versus floor 1.5 (per-class: crypto 1.69, politics 1.75, sports 1.74, other 1.70 — all four classes pass independently). Median terminal jump magnitude |∆It |pooled = 0.50 versus floor 0.10, identical to four significant figures across two independent passes covering disjoint cohorts. The terminal-jump finding empirically anchors the central design argument: the median resolved market in the empirical window collapses from It ∈ (0.45, 0.55) at τ − 1 h to R ∈ {0, 1} at τ , a magnitude of price jump that continuous-volatility static margin cannot

absorb without forcing L = 1. A pre-registered prediction on resolution-time depth contraction failed on its registered total-depth measure; the ±50 basis-point near-mid depth measure entered the analysis as a post-failure diagnostic and sensitivity lens, not as a structural premise of the failure-mode propositions. See Section 8.1.

E2 and E3 counterfactual replay (three of five pre-registered materiality floors fail; two pass). The five pre-registered floors and their realised values are:

• E2a liquidation-rate reduction: −6% pooled versus floor −30% (fails).

• E2b drawdown reduction: −5.1% pooled (crypto class −11.1%) versus floor −50% (fails).

• E2c median synthetic-trader PnL direction: +14% (passes direction).

• E3 Floor 1 final-hour liquidation-rate reduction: −80.4% versus floor −50% (passes; mechanically by halt construction).

• E3 Floor 2 bad-debt frequency reduction: +2.4% versus floor −75% (fails).

The three failed floors are documented per the pre-registration discipline. Two design lessons extracted from the failures are reported as contributions in their own right: that the resolution-zone halt protocol addresses execution-channel liquidation risk but does not address terminal-jump bad-debt risk (which lives in the margin schedule, not the halt protocol; Section 9.11); and that dynamic-margin reaction pre-empts more recoveries than it prevents on observed paths — a structural trade-off replicated across the E2 and E3 counterfactual replays (Section 9.10). Cross-class generalisation beyond sports is constrained by sports dominance (77.9% of three-class total) and a 17.4% within-window resolution ceiling.

1.6 Scope and limitations of empirical claims We state explicitly what the paper does and does not do, in declarative form, because the appropriate scope of an empirical paper on a non-existent product is unusually delicate.

What this paper does. It develops and evaluates a specific risk-engine design for a specific instrument (PIRAP) on a specific data source (Polymarket v2 archive). It documents structural failure modes of the naive crypto-perp transplant, develops a framework that addresses each, and measures the framework’s behavior under counterfactual replay against observed paths. It produces a listing eligibility framework grounded in observable market features. It identifies four directions for future research that would extend the empirical evidence base.

What this paper does not do.

• It does not claim balanced cross-class evidence on Polymarket. The pre-registered Sample Adequacy Gate triggered the sports-dominance consequence rule on the stratified-byday analysis sample (sports share 77.9%, above the 70% threshold; Section 5.5). The chronological-prefix subsamples we ran first showed an even more extreme trajectory (74.6% on 15K, 89.3% on 50K), which the day-1 selection-bias finding identified as chronological artifact; the stratified sample correction returns 77.9%, intermediate between the two chronological figures and firmly above the trigger threshold. Sports dominance is therefore a structural property of the empirical week’s market mix on Polymarket, not a single-day artifact. The paper’s primary empirical claims are sportsanchored; politics and crypto are reported as secondary classes documenting framework behavior on classes other than the dominant one. Broad cross-class generalization claims are explicitly weakened where this matters (Sections 8 and 9.2).

Empirical scope and the data window. The empirical analysis is bounded below by the start of the PMXT v2 archive on 2026-04-13. The reader should treat empirical claims as Polymarket-specific and window-specific. Generalization to other venues, other windows, or other event mixes requires replication.

1.7 Roadmap The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in prediction markets, perpetual futures mechanism design, and bounded-process modeling. Section 3 introduces the formal setting: the binary-event price process, notation, and the Polymarket platform context. Section 4 states the data integrity and reproducibility commitments. Section 5 describes the data sources, sample selection, cleaning, sample adequacy gate, and stylized facts. Section 6 establishes the formal non-portability propositions. Section 7 develops the resolution-aware framework. Section 8 reports empirical evaluation across E1, E2, and E3. Section 9 states limitations. Section 10 sets out a future research agenda for extending the empirical evidence base. Section 11 summarizes and outlines the companion-paper agenda.

We do not attempt a comprehensive survey; we identify the references most directly load-bearing for the paper’s framework and empirical strategy. agenda. 2 Related Work This section positions the paper relative to four bodies of work: prediction-market microstructure (Section 2.1), perpetual-futures mechanism design and funding rates (Section 2.2), liquidation dynamics in leveraged crypto markets (Section 2.3), and informed-trading theory in event-driven settings (Section 2.4). We do not attempt a comprehensive survey; we identify the references most directly load-bearing for the paper’s framework and empirical strategy. Three adjacent literatures — bounded-process pricing models, oracle manipulation, and gambling/financial-contract distinctions — are relevant but not surveyed here; we cite them where the argument requires.

2.1 Prediction-market microstructure on CLOB venues The empirical literature on prediction markets has historically focused on price-level questions: forecast accuracy, calibration against realized outcomes, the longshot bias, and the extent to which informed and uninformed traders coexist on the same venue (Manski, 2006; Wolfers and Zitzewitz, 2004). This price-level focus reflects the data available from the early venues, which used scoring rules (Hanson, 2003) or sparse parimutuel pools and exposed limited continuous order-book data. The trading mechanism mattered less than the price as an aggregator. CLOB-based prediction markets, of which Polymarket is the prominent recent example, change this picture. The CLOB exposes continuous depth, spread, latency, and trade-tape data at the same granularity as conventional spot exchanges, which makes the microstructure questions tractable for the first time at scale. Two recent contributions are central to our setting. Dubach, 2026 provides the most detailed microstructure characterization of the Polymarket order book to date, covering 30 billion events over 52 days on a pre-registered 600-market panel and reporting eight stylized facts including a longshot spread premium, a depth-concentration profile closer to a uniform geometric grid than to the top-of-book pattern often assumed for prediction markets, and category-conditional differences in effective spread. Tsang and Yang, 2026 provides a transaction-level decomposition of the 2024 US election cycle on Polymarket, focusing on trader behavior, market disagreement, and manipulation risk. Rahman et al., 2025 provides a systematization-of-knowledge survey of decentralized prediction market designs and their trade-offs around decentralization, expressiveness, and manipulation resistance. Our paper differs from each in scope. Dubach is descriptive across the entire venue and does not consider derivative overlay; the 2024 election anatomy is event-cycle-specific and does not consider leveraged margin design; the SoK paper is design-space-focused and does not develop a quantitative risk-engine framework. We use Dubach (2026) primarily as a benchmark for the stylized facts we report in Section 5: where the two samples overlap (CLOB venue, similar event mix), our facts should be broadly consistent. Disagreements would themselves be informative. The earlier scoring-rule literature, beginning with Hanson, 2003, deserves more careful engagement than a forward-pointer to its successors. The Logarithmic Market Scoring Rule established three results that remain directly relevant to any prediction-market design, including CLOB-based ones. First, the liquidity parameter b in LMSR provides bounded worst-case loss to the market maker, a property that CLOB venues do not inherit automatically and that motivates separate design discipline (in our setting, the boundary funding correction of Section 7.5 is in part a substitute for the bounded-loss guarantee that LMSR provides through its cost function). Second, LMSR is associated with a manipulation-cost framework: the cost to an adversary of moving the price by a fixed amount is bounded below in a manner that depends on b (Chen et al., 2010, 2011). A CLOB venue with a derivative overlay does not inherit this manipulation-cost guarantee, and our composite robust index in Section 7.2 is in part a response to that gap. Third, LMSR’s path-independence and information-aggregation

properties are features of the cost function, not of the trading venue, and a CLOB-based prediction market gives them up in exchange for direct trader-to-trader liquidity provision. The point is not that LMSR has been superseded; the point is that CLOB-based venues solve a different problem, and the design discipline that LMSR encodes (bounded loss, manipulation cost, information aggregation) must be either reconstructed or relaxed in the new setting. Our framework reconstructs bounded-loss and manipulation-cost discipline through the index and margin specifications in Section 7; we do not address path independence or formal information aggregation, which we treat as out of scope.

2.2 Perpetual-futures mechanism and funding rates Perpetual futures (perpetual swaps) emerged in cryptocurrency markets in 2016 with BitMEX’s introduction of the inverse bitcoin perpetual. The mechanism is, in summary, a margincollateralized non-expiring contract whose price is tethered to a reference index via periodic funding payments between long and short positions, with the funding rate proportional to (a function of) the basis between perp and index. The mechanism has become the dominant derivative structure in crypto, with daily volumes exceeding 100 billion USD across major venues by 2024. Despite the centrality of the instrument, academic mechanism analysis is comparatively recent. He et al., 2024 develops the canonical no-arbitrage relationship between perpetual price, spot price, and funding rate, providing the theoretical foundation against which mechanism deviations can be measured. Dai et al., 2025 extends this to the case where the funding mechanism includes a clamping function (capped funding rate), deriving model-free noarbitrage bounds and showing that persistent price discrepancies cannot be explained by transaction fees alone. Zhang, 2026 treats the funding rate as an algorithmic feedback rule rather than a passive transfer, deriving stability conditions in a continuous-time equilibrium with risk-constrained arbitrageurs and momentum speculators, and analyzing the effect of funding-rate caps, clamp-style piecewise-linear rules, and jump-and-crisis extensions with liquidation-driven crashes. Empirical work on funding-rate dynamics is sparser. The earliest systematic analysis we are aware of is Nimmagadda and Sasanka, 2019, which documents the heteroskedastic nature of BitMEX funding rates and establishes Granger-causal relationships between funding and the inverse perpetual price. More recent work (“Exploring Risk and Return Profiles of Funding Rate Arbitrage on CEX and DEX” 2025) examines funding-rate arbitrage profiles across CEX and DEX venues for major cryptocurrencies. Giagkiozis and Said, 2024 reconciles open interest with traded volume in perpetual swaps, providing a method to estimate collateral requirements at exchange scale. These references jointly motivate two design decisions in our framework. First, the basisonly funding rule of the naive crypto-perp port (Definition 1) is the canonical mechanism analyzed in He et al. (2024) and Zhang (2026); it is the natural baseline to attack. Second, the boundary-correction term in our funding rule (Definition 6) is in the same family as the modifications Dai et al. (2025) discuss for clamping functions, but parameterized on the index region rather than on the funding magnitude.

2.3 Liquidation dynamics and optimal margin under leverage The empirical literature on crypto-perpetual liquidations documents both the frequency of forced liquidation events and the cascade dynamics under stress. Cheng et al., 2021 applies generalized extreme value theory to BitMEX perpetual data and finds that 3.51% of long positions and 1.89% of short positions face forced liquidation on a daily basis at the venue’s prevailing margin rules, with average leverage among liquidated positions of 60X. They recommend tightening initial margin requirements substantially — to 33% (3X leverage) for

longs and 20% (5X) for shorts — to bring the daily margin call probability down to 1%. This is one of the few empirical anchors for what constitutes prudent margin design under high-leverage crypto-perp conditions. Ali, 2025 provides an event study of the October 10–11, 2025 crypto liquidation cascade, in which roughly 19 billion USD of open interest was erased within 36 hours after a macroeconomicpolicy trigger. The paper documents reflexive feedback loops between leverage, liquidity, and volatility and identifies the microstructure channels through which forced liquidations amplify price moves. The November 2025 BTC cascade described in industry commentary is a smaller but similar episode in the same year. See, e.g., the Coinchange Q4 2025 review and the AMINA Bank Q3 2025 derivatives report. (industry signal; Section F) These references inform two of our design components. The leverage-compression schedule (Definition 5) is calibrated against the Cheng et al. (2021) recommendation of 3X–5X effective leverage at high-stress regimes; our schedule imposes Lmax (t) → 1 as (T − t) → 0, which is more aggressive in the resolution-zone but consistent in spirit. The anti-cascade dampening protocol (Section 7.6) is a direct response to the reflexive-feedback dynamic documented in Ali (2025).

2.4 Informed trading and adverse selection in event markets The market microstructure tradition starting with Kyle, 1985 and Glosten and Milgrom, 1985 models price formation under asymmetric information between informed and uninformed traders. The core insight — that bid-ask spreads compensate market makers for adverseselection risk against informed trades — carries over to prediction-market settings, with two complications. First, prediction markets resolve at known terminal states, so the informed-trader’s information edge is bounded in time. Second, the information that matters for binary-event prices is often event-specific (the outcome of a sports match, the result of an election) rather than fundamental, which changes the structure of information flow. We do not develop a formal model of informed trading on event markets in this paper; we use the Kyle-GM framework as background motivation for why bid-ask spreads might widen in boundary regions where information is more concentrated, and we defer formal modeling to future work.

2.5 Adjacent literatures we do not survey here Four adjacent bodies of work are relevant but secondary to this paper’s central argument. We cite them where the argument requires and do not attempt a survey. Bounded-process pricing models (the canonical reference being Cox et al., 1985 on absorbing-barrier interestrate processes) are relevant to the formal price-process treatment in Section 3.1, but our setting (two-sided absorbing boundaries with terminal collapse to {0, 1}) differs from the CIR class in ways that make direct inheritance limited; we use it as a conceptual reference, not a foundational dependency. Oracle manipulation literature (UMA papers, oracle-attack analyses) bears on Section 7.2 but our manipulation analysis is primarily empirical and does not require formal oracle modeling. Gambling vs. financial-contract distinctions in law and economics are relevant to the framing of Section 9.6 but require legal expertise we do not claim. Welfare analyses of derivative-market introduction (Hart, Allen-Gale) are relevant to the broader question of whether ELPs improve market efficiency but not to this paper’s narrower risk-engine focus; companion papers (Paper 2 and Paper 3 in our planned series) address those questions more directly.

Section 3.1 characterizes the underlying price process at the level of generality required for the design and analysis that follow. Section 3.2 fixes notation; the full glossary is in Appendix A. Section 3.3 describes the Polymarket venue from which our empirical observations are drawn.

3.1 The binary-event price process Let E denote a binary event with two mutually exclusive outcomes, indexed by R ∈ {0, 1}. Resolution occurs at a time τ . For some event classes τ is scheduled (e.g., a sports match finishing at a known time); for others it is a random stopping time (e.g., a political event that may or may not occur by a deadline). We denote by T the time the engine treats as scheduled or expected resolution, which need not equal τ . A prediction-market venue trades a contract that pays $1 if R = 1 and $0 if R = 0. We denote by pt ∈ [0, 1] the time-t price of this contract on the venue. We treat pt as a market signal, not a probability. The distinction matters: pt reflects the marginal trader’s willingness to pay under the venue’s particular order-book state, fee schedule, capital constraints, and information set. It is contaminated by liquidity premia, manipulation pressure, and funding distortions in ways that the literature on prediction-market pricing has documented at length (see Wolfers and Zitzewitz, 2004, Manski, 2006). For the design and empirical analysis below, we require only that pt is observable, bounded in [0, 1], and collapses discretely to R ∈ {0, 1} at τ in the sense that limt↑τ pt may differ from R by an arbitrary amount in [−1, 1]. This process has four features that distinguish it from an unbounded spot-asset price. The empirical work in Section 5 examines these features quantitatively; here we state them as the design assumptions our framework is built around.

Bounded support with terminal collapse. The process pt takes values in the closed unit interval, in contrast to spot crypto and equity prices which take values in R+ . At τ , the process collapses to one of the two endpoints. This collapse is not the end of a continuous trajectory; it is a discontinuous jump whose magnitude is the distance between limt↑τ pt and R. The discontinuous-jump component of the process aligns with classical jump-diffusion modeling (Merton, 1976), modified here by the boundedness of the support: jumps are constrained to land within [0, 1] and the terminal jump lands exactly at {0, 1}.

Information-driven jump intensity. Jump arrival in pt is not Poisson with calendar-time intensity. It is concentrated on information-arrival times that are partly endogenous (debate moments, goals scored, statistical disclosures) and partly exogenous (unforeseen news). The implication for engine design is that π̂tjump , the engine’s estimator of jump probability over the current margin horizon, must be conditional on observable proxies for information arrival rather than calibrated as a stationary parameter. We define π̂tjump as a dimensionless probability rather than a calendar-time intensity for consistency with the margin formulae of Section 7.3, where it multiplies a notional position size to produce a margin add-on.

Thin liquidity in the tails. Empirically (Section 5), order-book depth Dt varies systematically with the region of pt . Markets where pt ∈ [0, 0.05] ∪ [0.95, 1] exhibit different spread and depth profiles than markets in the interior. Engines that assume depth is independent of price level will misprice both manipulation cost and liquidation safety margin.

Resolution-time clustering. Liquidity, trading activity, and information arrivals all cluster around τ . In a sports market, final-minute events dominate; in a political event with a scheduled deadline, the last hours carry disproportionate news weight. Risk parameters that ignore (τ − t) underestimate this clustering’s contribution to liquidation severity. These four features motivate the central design claim of the paper: a risk engine for an ELP on this process must be resolution-aware by construction.

3.2 Notation and state variables We track the following state variables. The full glossary is in Appendix A; the variables introduced in Section 7 (engine outputs) are also defined there. • pt ∈ [0, 1] — prediction-market reference price for E. • It ∈ [0, 1] — index price computed by the engine from observable market data; specified in Section 7.2. • qt — mark price on the perp venue. • Ft — funding rate at time t. • Mtinit , Mtmaint — initial and maintenance margin schedules. • Lmax (t) — maximum allowable leverage at time t. • σt — realized volatility of pt over a windowed estimator; σ̂t denotes the engine’s estimator. • π̂tjump — engine estimator of the probability of a terminal jump within the current margin horizon, conditional on observable signals; defined precisely in Appendix C. Dimensionless, in [0, 1]. • Dt — depth metric: total quoted size within ±200 bps of It . • OIt — open interest on the perp. • Λt — liquidation pressure, the notional currently in the liquidation queue. • κt — engine’s lower-bound estimate of the cost required to displace It by a stated amount, derived from observed depth. • ρt — resolution-clarity score, a proxy for oracle and dispute risk. • SEA , BE — listing eligibility components defined in Section 7.8 and Section 7.9. The notation above is canonical for the entire paper. We do not introduce parallel symbols for the same quantity in any section.

3.3 The platform context: Polymarket as a CLOB-based event venue Our empirical observations are drawn exclusively from Polymarket, a prediction-market platform settling binary events on the Polygon network. We summarize the platform structure to the depth needed for the analysis; the empirical scope statements in Section 1.6 clarify what does and does not generalize beyond Polymarket without replication.

Order book. Polymarket operates a central limit order book (CLOB) for each market. Each binary event has two outcome tokens (YES and NO), and quotes for both tokens form complementary order books. Trading is collateralized in USDC. This is in contrast to LMSRbased prediction markets which use a market-maker scoring rule to provide continuous liquidity; Polymarket relies on traditional limit-order liquidity provision.

Resolution. Markets are resolved through UMA’s Optimistic Oracle (OO) protocol on Polygon. A whitelisted proposer posts the outcome; if no dispute arrives within a liveness window, the proposal settles and the market resolves. As of mid-2026, two oracle infrastructures coexist within Polymarket’s adapter ecosystem: standard UMA OOv2 (0xee3afe...), used for long-horizon legacy markets; and Managed OOv2 (MOOV2, 0x2c0367...), introduced under UMIP-189 and used for new short-horizon markets, where proposers are restricted to a managed whitelist with documented reliability records. The empirical sample of this paper is operationally dominated by MOOV2: Section 9.3 documents the observed >99% MOOV2 share and its implications, including the consequence that dispute frequency (an input to BE ) carries less information than it would in a venue with active OOv2/MOOV2 co-dominance.

Data. The PMXT v2 public archive provides hourly Parquet dumps of the Polymarket CLOB WebSocket event stream. Each file contains tick-level events with millisecond timestamps for four event types: book (full L2 snapshot, sparse), price_change (quote update with best bid/ask, dominant), last_trade_price (trade execution with size, side, fee, transaction hash), and tick_size_change (rare). Coverage begins 2026-04-13T19 UTC, which bounds the empirical window of this paper. Section 5 describes the schema, sample selection, and cleaning procedures in detail; Appendix B gives the full schema. We do not claim Polymarket-specific findings transfer to Kalshi or other CLOB-based event venues without replication. The framework developed in Section 7 is platform-agnostic by construction; the empirical findings in Section 8 are not.

4 Data Integrity and Reproducibility This section describes how the empirical analysis was conducted, what synthetic components appear and where they are isolated, and what reproducibility commitments hold. We place this section before the data and stylized facts (Section 5) because the empirical discipline matters before the empirical content does. A reader who agrees with the principles below should find every result downstream either deterministic from observed data or explicitly labeled as a calibrated counterfactual.

4.1 Principles The analysis follows ten principles. They are stated declaratively here because they shape every choice in Sections 5, 8 and 10.

1. Data-first. The empirical backbone is historical Polymarket order-book and trade data. Synthetic or Monte Carlo evidence is never primary.

2. No fabricated observations. All time-series in figures and tables come from observed data or from deterministic computations on observed data.

3. Synthetic components are isolated, labeled, calibrated, and confined to the robustness layer. The only synthetic element used anywhere in the paper is the trader-population layer in experiment E2c (Section 8.2.3). The main results of E2 (positions-agnostic survivability and the deterministic position grid) do not depend on it.

4. Counterfactual replay, not simulation. Hypothetical engine configurations are evaluated by feeding observed market paths into deterministic engine rules. We do not generate synthetic paths and evaluate engines on them.

5. Falsifiability stated in advance, with floors not slogans. Each empirical claim has a stated falsification criterion. Where multi-objective trade-offs exist, the criterion

specifies floors on each axis ex ante. Section 8.3 gives the welfare and continuity floors for E3, pre-registered in Appendix C.

6. Parameters are either estimated from observable data or explicitly treated as policy parameters. No engine parameter is hand-tuned without disclosure. Every policy parameter is varied in robustness analysis with a documented sensitivity range. Appendix C lists which is which.

7. Polymarket-specific empirical scope, platform-agnostic framework. All empirical claims are Polymarket-specific until replicated on other venues. The risk-engine framework is constructed to be platform-agnostic; it can be re-applied on Kalshi or other CLOB-based event venues, and we encourage that replication.

4.2 Pipeline separation The processing pipeline is separated into four named stages, each producing typed intermediate artifacts:

1. Raw ingest. PMXT v2 archive Parquet files are downloaded to local disk, validated for byte-level integrity (size and parquet metadata), and listed in a SHA-256 manifest. Resolution metadata is fetched from UMA Optimistic Oracle records via the Goldskyhosted subgraph (for OOv2-resolved markets) and via Polymarket’s Gamma API (for MOOV2-resolved markets). Market metadata is fetched from the Gamma API.

2. Cleaning. Schema enforcement, deduplication, timestamp normalization, stale-quote detection, broken-market filtering, outcome-resolution validation. The cleaning step is documented in Appendix B.7.

3. Feature construction. Spread, depth, jump detection, news-window labeling (where Augmentation gate G4 is satisfied), and engine inputs computed per Appendix C.

4. Engine evaluation. The risk-engine rules of Section 7 applied to observed paths under three configurations C0, C1, C2. Outputs are deterministic given observed inputs and stated rules.

The four stages are implemented in distinct code modules under the public repository (Section 4.4); they communicate via on-disk artifacts rather than in-memory state, so any stage can be re-run independently from cached outputs of earlier stages.

4.3 Seeds, hashes, and version pinning Every script logs at execution time:

• Git SHA of the repository.

• Pinned versions of all Python dependencies relevant to the computation (polars, httpx, pyarrow, web3, pycryptodome).

• Random seed where any randomness enters the computation (E2c trader-population sampling, bootstrap confidence intervals).

• SHA-256 hashes of input data files.

• Timestamp of execution in UTC.

These metadata fields are written into every output artifact (Parquet files, JSON reports, intermediate dataframes serialized to disk). A reader who downloads the public repository at the same git SHA, with the same dependency versions and the same input file hashes, must obtain identical outputs.

4.4 Public release The following are published alongside the paper at a public repository (URL in the camera-ready version):

• Source code for all four pipeline stages.

• Data schema for the PMXT v2 archive (Appendix B).

• Summary statistics and parameter tables for every figure and table in the paper.

• Sample data sufficient to reproduce a representative subset of results.

• SHA-256 hashes of all input files used in the published run.

• Reconstruction procedure for files we cannot redistribute.

The public PMXT v2 archive is the source for the primary data layer. Where Polymarket terms of service prevent redistribution of derived data, we provide reconstruction procedures that any reader can execute against the public archive, the public Gamma API, and the public UMA oracle infrastructure.

4.5 Synthetic component enumeration We enumerate every synthetic element that appears anywhere in the paper, so a reader who rejects all synthetic-data-driven claims still knows precisely which results survive.

Trader-population layer in E2c. The only synthetic element in the paper is the trader population in experiment E2c (Section 8.2.3). It comprises N synthetic traders with a leverage distribution calibrated to publicly documented crypto-perp leverage histograms (cited in Section 8.2.3), and entry/exit decisions modeled as a thresholded process on observable signals. The role of E2c is bounded: it serves as a robustness layer to confirm or refute the enginecomparison findings of E2a (positions-agnostic survivability) and E2b (deterministic position grid) under heterogeneous-position aggregation. E2a and E2b are trader-independent: they evaluate the engine rules against observed price paths without assuming any particular trader population. The main empirical claims of Section 8.2 rest on E2a and E2b. A reader who rejects E2c entirely retains E2a and E2b as the basis for the resolution-aware framework’s empirical justification.

5 Data and Stylized Facts This section describes the data on which the paper’s empirical analysis runs. It establishes coverage, integrity, and the population of markets available for downstream analysis. Subsections 5.1 through 5.3 cover the data architecture and the structural finding about archive accessibility that emerged during ingestion. Section 5.4 describes the sample adequacy gate as a methodological commitment; the gate’s empirical evaluation on the classification-enriched market population is reported in Section 5.5 once the metadata-enrichment run completes. 5.1 Data sources The empirical work uses three public data sources, joined under explicit version constants and adapter registries.

Primary source: PMXT v2 archive. Hourly-partitioned Parquet files containing the Polymarket CLOB WebSocket event stream at tick granularity. The schema includes four event types (book, price_change, last_trade_price, tick_size_change) with millisecond timestamps. The full column schema is documented in Appendix B.1. We emphasize that these are tick-level events, not hourly snapshots: a single hour’s file contains every order-book update, every trade, and every tick-size change for every active market in that hour. The trade tape (last_trade_price events) is included in the primary archive; no separate trade-tape augmentation is required. This was confirmed during ingestion module CC- 001 (see ingest/uma_resolutions.py and the corresponding adapter documentation in the repository).

Resolution metadata. UMA Optimistic Oracle records on Polygon. Two adapter mechanisms are active in the empirical window: the standard UMA Optimistic Oracle V2 (OOv2) for long-horizon markets created before the August 2025 governance migration, and the Managed Optimistic Oracle V2 (MOOV2) introduced under UMIP-189 for new short-horizon markets. The two require different access paths: OOv2 records are queried via Goldsky subgraph; MOOV2 records are accessed via Polymarket’s Gamma API outcomePrices field. The adapter registry is locked at ADAPTER_REGISTRY_VERSION = 2026-05-05 in ingest/uma_resolutions.py. The implications of mechanism heterogeneity for the empirical analysis are discussed in Section 9.3.

Market metadata. Polymarket Gamma API for market title, tags, outcome tokens, scheduled resolution date, and resolution status. The PMXT-to-Gamma join is by asset_id = exact ASCII-string match against clobTokenIds. Event-class classification rule is locked at EVENT_CLASS_RULE_VERSION = v1 in ingest/market_metadata.py.

Cleaning. Each PMXT event has a timestamp_received (server ingestion time) and a timestamp (event authoring time). We use timestamp_received as the primary sort key; timestamp appears only for diagnostic purposes (latency analysis). Out-of-order or duplicate events within a market are detected on a second-pass scan and dropped. The percentage of events dropped under this rule is reported per file in Section 5.5.

The 2024 US Presidential Election cycle, the most-cited Polymarket event in the public discussion of prediction markets, is therefore outside the empirical window. We discuss the implications in Section 9.1. The primary empirical window of this paper is the calendar week 2026-04-21T00 UTC through 2026-04-27T23 UTC — 168 contiguous hours selected as the first complete Monday-toSunday week available in the archive. The week was chosen ex ante to provide coverage across both weekday-active markets (politics, macro) and weekend-active markets (sports finals), and to provide a clean calendar boundary that supports straightforward replication. 5.3 Archive structure: a finding from ingestion During the ingestion work for this paper, an architectural feature of the public PMXT v2 archive emerged that is worth documenting because it bears on reproducibility. PMXT exposes its archive through two distinct endpoints with materially different behavior. The first is an HTML index at https://archive.pmxt.dev/Polymarket/v2, designed for

human browsing, which paginates a rolling window of approximately 100 files at any given time. The second is the underlying R2 storage at https://r2v2.pmxt.dev/polymarket_ orderbook_<YYYY-MM-DDTHH>.parquet, which is permanent and complete from the archive start (2026-04-13T19 UTC) onward. The two endpoints can produce different views of the same archive: a researcher who paginates the HTML index on a given day will see only files from approximately the past four days. A researcher who enumerates URLs against R2 directly will retrieve every file ever published. Our downloader uses direct R2 enumeration; the canonicality of the resulting file set is verified in our committed MANIFEST.sha256 artifact for the primary window. The implication for reproducibility is operational. We state it as a rule:

Replication rule for the PMXT v2 archive. Do not paginate the HTML index at archive.pmxt.dev as the canonical file list. Enumerate hourly URLs against r2v2.pmxt.dev/polymarket_orderbook_<YYYY-MM-DDTHH>.parquet by UTC hour for the desired date range, and verify every file against the committed MANIFEST.sha256.

This rule is implemented by our downloader (ingest/download_archive.py) and is the canonical access pattern for any researcher reproducing or extending this work. We note dualendpoint access patterns are a structural feature of public-data infrastructure on Polymarketclass venues that future microstructure researchers should be aware of, and the reason that committed cryptographic manifests — rather than “download from the same URL” instructions — are the correct reproducibility primitive for time-series venue data. We do not characterize this dual-endpoint behavior as a defect of PMXT. The HTML index appears designed for casual browsing and the R2 endpoint for programmatic access; the design is reasonable, but the distinction is not currently documented in either endpoint’s surface text and was discovered empirically.

5.4 Sample adequacy gate The Sample Adequacy Gate (G5) is a pre-registered methodological commitment from plan v1.2 §5.4: before any empirical claim is made in this paper, the gate is evaluated against the ingested data and its consequence rules are applied. The gate is not a quality-control checkbox; it is a structural commitment that the paper’s empirical positioning is determined by what the data supports, not by what was intended at the outset.

Gate measurements. For each event class (politics, sports, crypto), the gate measures the count of usable resolved markets satisfying: (i) sufficient observed lifetime (≥ 24 h within the window), (ii) successful join to Gamma metadata yielding event-class label, (iii) successful join to UMA / Gamma resolution yielding terminal outcome R ∈ {0, 1}, and (iv) non-degenerate event density (median trades per hour above a documented floor).

Pre-registered consequence rules (plan v1.2 §5.4.2). The empirical positioning of the paper is determined by which of three rule branches the gate triggers:

• Full three-class panel. If npolitics ≥ 20, nsports ≥ 20, ncrypto ≥ 50, and total n ≥ 100: the paper proceeds with the full three-class empirical evaluation as designed. The higher crypto floor (n ≥ 50) reflects that crypto markets on Polymarket include both threshold markets (BTC above some price by some date) and many short-horizon variants of related questions, so a larger sample is required to avoid treating near-duplicate markets as independent observations in the cross-class comparison.

Sports-share trigger fired on the stratified analysis sample, confirming the structural pattern. The sports share of 77.9% on the stratified sample exceeds the 70% preregistered trigger threshold. We initially saw this trigger fire at 74.6% on the 15,000-market chronological subsample (CC-003.9). The 50,000-market chronological subsample showed a more extreme 89.3%, which we suspected was due to day-1 selection bias. The stratifiedby-day sample, which corrects for that bias, returns 77.9% — intermediate between the two chronological figures and firmly above the trigger threshold. Excluding Apr 21 entirely from the stratified composition still yields 72.6% sports share, confirming that sports dominance is a structural property of the empirical week’s market mix on Polymarket, not a single-day artifact. The pre-registered consequence is that the paper’s primary cross-class empirical claims are sports-anchored. Politics and crypto are reported as secondary classes that document framework behavior on classes other than the dominant one. Broad prediction-market generalization claims are explicitly weakened where they would otherwise rest on under-represented class evidence. This is the discipline working as designed: the consequence rule existed precisely because we did not know ex ante whether the week’s mix would be balanced or sports-dominant; the stratified sample shows it is sports-dominant, and we apply the consequence honestly.

Late-week structural artifacts. Two structural features of the analysis sample warrant explicit documentation:

• Apr 27 (last day of the empirical window) contributes 0 usable markets. Markets first observed on Apr 27 had observed lifetimes ≤ 23.97h, just below the 24-hour gate floor. This is a window-edge effect: the gate filters the last day’s brand-new markets from the analysis sample because they have not had time to develop the activity density required for usability.

• Apr 26 contributes 0 usable politics markets. Late-week political markets in this empirical window had not yet resolved within the window itself, so they did not pass the UMAresolution-join gate. This is consistent with the general resolution-window structural ceiling discussed below.

These edge effects do not weaken the analysis: the analysis sample of 13,298 usable markets is large by any standard, distributed across days 1–6 of the week, and the structural reasons for the day-7 and Apr-26-politics gaps are documented.

Resolution-window structural ceiling. The structural ceiling on resolution-conditional analyses — the fraction of sampled markets whose resolution timestamp falls within the empirical window — was reported as 27.3% on the 15,000-market chronological subsample (4,091 / 15,000 markets resolved within the 168-hour window). The 1,000-market chronological subsample reported 34.6%; the 50,000-market chronological subsample revealed an even more extreme pattern: roughly 79% of those 50,000 markets had observed lifetimes exceeding the 168-hour archive window itself, indicating they were created before the window and dragged into it, not opened-and-closed within it. None of the 50,000 day-1 markets opened and closed within 24 hours. The chronological-prefix selection therefore produces a non-representative resolution-ceiling measurement. The stratified analysis sample yields a ceiling of 17.4% (the fraction of stratifiedsample markets resolving within the 168-hour window). This is substantially lower than any of the chronological estimates, because the chronological subsamples over-represented markets created within the window (which are more likely to also resolve within it), while the stratified sample includes a representative fraction of long-horizon markets created before the window. The 17.4% figure is the value used in Section 9.7.

Sample-count progression. For clarity across the empirical evaluation, three sample sizes recur: 61,087 markets ingested under the stratified-by-day rule (target 70K, actual 61,087); 13,298 markets passing adequacy gates and constituting the analysis sample for E1/E2/SF1– SF9 (the value labeled “Total usable” in Table 3); and 13,115 markets in the analysis sample that additionally resolved within the 168-hour empirical window, the subset on which CC-008 (E3) evaluates the resolution-zone protocol. The 17.4% ceiling above is computed against the 61,087-market stratified-sample denominator and reflects the broader question of how many ingested markets reach resolution within a single-week window; it is a different ratio from 13,115 / 13,298 (the within-window fraction of the analysis sample, which is high because the adequacy gates pre-filter for markets with sufficient event-history data).

Oracle source distribution: de facto single-mechanism in the empirical window. The CC-003.10 50,000-market subsample revealed a finding worth flagging: 99.8% of resolutions in the subsample came through the Managed Optimistic Oracle V2 (MOOV2, accessed via Gamma’s outcomePrices field), with <0.2% through the legacy UMA Optimistic Oracle V2 (OOv2). For the empirical window 2026-04-21 to 2026-04-27, Polymarket has effectively migrated to MOOV2 as the operational oracle for new markets; OOv2 is retained for residual long-horizon markets created before the August 2025 governance migration but plays a negligible role in the analysis sample. The implication for the oracle-mechanism heterogeneity discussion in Section 9.3 is that the comparison between OOv2 and MOOV2 populations is not an active concern in our window: we are working with a de facto single-oracle sample. The dispute-frequency baseline documented in Section 9.3 is therefore the MOOV2 baseline, not a mixed baseline. We retain the discussion of mechanism heterogeneity because it remains relevant to any cross-temporal or cross-platform extension of the framework, but it does not bear on Section 8 interpretation in the present paper.

5.6 Stylized facts on the analysis sample We report nine stylized facts on the stratified-by-day analysis sample, organized around the four framework dimensions whose empirical validity Section C flagged for E1 verification: boundary depth asymmetry (SF1), terminal jump magnitude (SF2), basis behavior near information arrival (SF3), effective spread conditional on the index region (SF4), order-book depth profile (SF5), trade size distribution (SF6), time-of-day activity (SF7), resolution-time activity surge (SF8), and resolution-time depth collapse (SF9). Each fact is reported both pooled across event classes and split by class, with attention to the sports-dominance constraint that limits broad cross-class generalization (Section 5.5). Per the falsifiability discipline of Section C.4, SF1 and SF2 are evaluated against preregistered floors. SF3–SF9 are descriptive: they characterize the analysis sample but do not have falsifiability thresholds attached. SF9 evaluates Empirical Condition 1 (resolution-time depth collapse) and informs the necessity argument for the framework’s leverage compression protocol but is not itself falsifiable in the same way SF1/SF2 are.

SF1: Boundary depth asymmetry. For markets in the boundary region It < δ = 0.10, we compute the within-book depth ratio ρ = Dtlong /Dtshort where Dtlong and Dtshort are displayed depths within ∆depth = 200 bps of the prevailing mid-price on each side. The pre-registered floor (Section C.4) is ρfloor = 1.5 at the median market. The pooled median across the analysis sample is ρpooled = 1.72 on base coverage (4,030 markets, files 1–121) and 1.65 on resume coverage (1,648 markets, files 122–168). Both passes exceed the floor independently. The per-class medians on base coverage are crypto 1.69, politics 1.75, sports 1.74, and other 1.70; all four classes pass the floor. The cross-pass and cross-class consistency confirms that boundary depth asymmetry is a structural property of the analysis sample, not an artifact of any specific subsample. SF1 passes; the asymmetry encoded in Assumption 3 is supported.

SF2: Terminal jump magnitude. For markets resolving within the empirical window, we compute the absolute change in It over the final hour before resolution: |∆It [τ − 1h, τ ]|. The pre-registered floor is a median of 0.10 at the median resolved market, evaluated both pooled and per-class. The pooled median is |∆It |pooled = 0.50, exceeding the pre-registered floor by a factor of five. The identical median is obtained independently on base coverage (6,012 markets resolving in files 1–121, |∆It | = 0.5000) and on resume coverage (4,225 markets resolving in files 122–168, |∆It | = 0.5000). Cross-pass coincidence to four significant figures confirms the finding is structural, not an artifact of any particular cohort. The substantive interpretation is striking. A median terminal jump of 50 percentage points means the typical resolved market in the empirical window transitions from It ∈ (0.45, 0.55) at τ − 1h to R ∈ {0, 1} at τ . By comparison, an equivalent jump in BTC or ETH crypto-perp markets would require a 50% terminal price move within an hour, which essentially never occurs. The bounded-event setting is qualitatively different: the terminal collapse is not a tail event but the median outcome at resolution. This empirically anchors the paper’s central design argument: Proposition 1 characterizes a continuous-vol static margin engine as unable to absorb the median bounded-event terminal jump without forcing L = 1, and the |∆It | = 0.5 finding shows that this is not a worst-case construction but the typical realized outcome in the analysis sample.

The 23% of resolved markets without a usable SF2 terminal observation (3,061 of 13,298 sample markets, 3,236 in the resume range specifically) represent markets whose terminalwindow quote streams contained no price-change events. A 50-market sanity sample (CC-006b) classifies all 50 as genuine illiquidity — zero observable price-change events and zero observable book updates in the final hour before resolution. The cohort is therefore not a computation gap; it is markets whose order books went completely dark before resolution. This classification is itself empirical support for the refined Empirical Condition 1 in Section 7: in nearly a quarter of the resolved sample, total displayed depth in the final hour is zero, a fortiori case of the refined "near-mid depth structurally absent" formulation. Class composition of the illiquidity cohort ("other" 43%, sports 35%, crypto 13%, politics 9%) is discussed in Section 9.8. We do not report per-class SF2 medians here. The base pass code emitted aggregate medians but not per-market terminal-jump values for the base-coverage markets, so per-class breakdown is available only for the 4,225 resume-coverage markets. Reporting per-class numbers on resume coverage alone would over-represent late-week markets and is not informative; reporting on combined coverage requires re-running base aggregation with the resume-pass per-market emission code, which is deferred. This measurement gap is documented in Section 9.8 alongside the classification gap.
